item.title: Celebrity dolphin of Venice doesn’t need special protection – except from humans
item.description: A dolphin returning to a historic habitat necessitates management of people, not wildlife, researchers monitoring solitary bottlenose dolphin in Venice say

item.title: Middle-aged men are most vulnerable to faster aging due to ‘forever chemicals’
item.description: Aging effect of specific PFAS is found to be greatest in men between 50 and 65

item.title: Sikt Renews National Open Access Agreement with Frontiers for 2026
item.description: Frontiers and the Norwegian Agency for Shared Services in Education and Research (Sikt) have announced the renewal of their national open access agreement for 2026. Originally signed in 2020, this partnership continues to streamline the publishing process for Norwegian researchers and reinforces the country's leadership in open access publishing.

item.title: Fossil amber reveals the secret lives of Cretaceous ants
item.description: Scientists use insects trapped in amber to understand ecosystems that died out millions of years ago

item.title: Modern twist on wildfire management methods found also to have a bonus feature that protects water supplies
item.description: Thinning to slow wildfires simultaneously boosts ‘hydrological resilience’ of forests

item.title: Chimps’ love for crystals could help us understand our own ancestors’ fascination with these stones
item.description: Ancestors of modern humans collected crystals for which they had no apparent use. A new chimp study could help researchers understand the roots of this infatuation.

item.title: How do you know you can trust the science you read?
item.description: It doesn’t happen by chance. Behind every article published in a Frontiers journal lies a structured, rigorous, seven-stage journey designed to safeguard integrity and protect the scientific record. At a time when scientific publishing faces growing challenges - from AI-generated and manufactured manuscripts to coordinated fraud - maintaining confidence in research has never been more important, demanding increasing vigilance at every step.

item.title: Narel Paniagua Zambrana – "You Cannot Conserve What You Do Not Know": Documenting Plant Knowledge to Protect Culture and Biodiversity
item.description: World Wildlife Day 2026 shines a spotlight on wild animals and plants, with this year's theme, “Medicinal and Aromatic Plants: Conserving Health, Heritage and Livelihoods.” To mark the day, we spoke with Dr Narel Paniagua Zambrana, an ethnobotanist whose career reflects both scientific leadership and the growing visibility of women in plant and environmental sciences. item.description: AI models generate meal plans that get necessary calories and macronutrients wrong, posing potential health risks to teenagers trying to lose weight
